Lessons.Title: Assess the Reasonableness of Solutions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Solve multi-step data problems using addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and careful estimates; check reasonableness of large-number answers. Data are drawn from historical classroom examples, not current population claims.

Original 2021 sequence: Notice and Wonder about the ten Native American language counts; Do You Speak Navajo?; Languages in Philadelphia and Chicago; synthesis. The original Children and the Elderly Cool-down is teacher-login restricted, so the Edulytics Cool-down below is independently authored.

2021 historical language table: Navajo 166,826; Yupik 19,750; Dakota 17,855; Apache 13,445; Keres 13,190; Cherokee 11,465; Ojibwa 9,735; Choctaw 9,635; Zuni 9,615; Pima 6,990. The graph must be treated as historical, and students check both additive and multiplicative comparisons.

Philadelphia historical source categories: English only 1,224,539; Spanish 127,352; other Indo-European 6,750; Asian 364. Chicago source categories include Spanish 422,568 and other Indo-European 25,777. The tables list selected categories, not a complete city census.

First-party independent Cool-down: 178,420 English-only speakers versus 35,680 Spanish and 12,900 other-language speakers. Combined non-English groups total 48,580, and the difference is 129,840. An estimate of about 130,000 is reasonable.

Original publisher bar graph and map are not reproduced. Independent numerical tables and equations support learner calculations; interpretation of historical source data, graph reading and estimation reasoning remain teacher-reviewed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Addition and subtraction of historical data
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use only the specified categories and counts; label years and units.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Find how many more with subtraction, and check by addition.
KeyConcepts.Example: 166,826 − 19,750 = 147,076 more Navajo speakers than Yupik in the source table.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reasonableness through benchmarks
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rounded estimate is a plausibility check on a precise multi-digit calculation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare rounded thousands or easy multiples before accepting a computed total.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare combined groups carefully
KeyConcepts.Definition: Sum every named category once before comparing cities or language groups.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check category inclusion and whether the question compares parts or totals.

WorkedExamples.Title: Navajo and Yupik: precise difference
WorkedExamples.Question: The 2021 source table has Navajo 166,826 speakers and Yupik 19,750. How many more speak Navajo?
Steps: Round to about 167,000 and 20,000 to anticipate about 147,000.

WorkedExamples.Title: Navajo and Yupik: multiplicative estimate
WorkedExamples.Question: About how many times as many Navajo speakers as Yupik speakers appear in the 2021 table?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare multiples and explain the estimate.
Steps: The observed 166,826 is nearer eight multiples, so about 8 times is a defensible whole-number estimate.
WorkedExamples.Check: 166,826 ÷ 19,750 ≈ 8.45; response is an estimate, not exact equality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Three languages in wartime context
WorkedExamples.Question: How many source-table speakers used Navajo, Apache or Cherokee?
WorkedExamples.Method: Add the three categories, not all ten.
Steps: List exactly the requested source counts: 166,826, 13,445 and 11,465.

WorkedExamples.Title: Navajo versus the other nine
WorkedExamples.Question: Were there more Navajo speakers than speakers of all other nine source-table languages combined?
WorkedExamples.Method: Sum and compare all specified categories.
Steps: Compare 166,826 Navajo speakers with 111,680 combined speakers.
166,826 − 111,680 = 55,146, so Navajo exceeds the nine combined.

WorkedExamples.Title: Philadelphia: English only versus other listed groups
WorkedExamples.Question: Using the selected Philadelphia source categories, what is the difference between English-only speakers and the other listed languages combined?
WorkedExamples.Method: Add the named language groups, then subtract.
Steps: The listed non-English source values are 127,352 + 6,750 + 364 = 134,466.

WorkedExamples.Title: Chicago versus Philadelphia: two language groups
WorkedExamples.Question: How many more source-table Spanish and other Indo-European speakers are in Chicago than Philadelphia?
WorkedExamples.Method: Keep the same two categories for both cities.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent Edulytics Cool-down
WorkedExamples.Question: A sample city survey gives 178,420 English-only speakers, 35,680 Spanish speakers and 12,900 other-language speakers. About how many more speak English only?
WorkedExamples.Method: Estimate, combine and subtract; first-party not publisher assessment.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Subtracting the two city counts without first combining the same language categories.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source question compares Spanish and other Indo-European speakers together.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Add both Chicago counts and both Philadelphia counts, then subtract 448,345 − 134,102.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating about eight times as exactly eight times, or counting Navajo twice in the nine-group total.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An approximate quotient need not equal exactly eight, and the other-nine sum excludes Navajo.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use 166,826 ÷ 19,750 ≈ 8.45 and verify the nine listed other languages total 111,680.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a selected historical table as an exhaustive or current national population count.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source has named historical categories and dates; it does not establish current totals.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use table values exactly for these maths exercises, name the scope, and avoid unsupported demographic claims.

SummaryPoints: 2021 Navajo − Yupik difference is 147,076; the ratio is about eight.
Navajo + Apache + Cherokee is 191,736; the other nine total 111,680, 55,146 fewer than Navajo.
Selected Philadelphia English-only versus other-language counts differ by 1,090,073.
Two matching language groups in Chicago exceed those in Philadelphia by 314,243.
The Edulytics Cool-down combines groups and subtracts: 178,420 − (35,680+12,900) = 129,840; teacher reviews source graphs and estimates.
